answer.label: Not Niels Bohr — actually John Gribbin
answer.sourceLine: The sentence comes from Gribbin’s 1984 popular-science book In Search of Schrödinger’s Cat (p. 211, as cited by Wikiquote ↗). There it sums up the quantum picture of reality. Later writers quoted it as Bohr’s own words. No Bohr source for this wording has been found.

trail: 1984 — John Gribbin’s In Search of Schrödinger’s Cat is published by Bantam Books (catalog record ↗). Wikiquote ↗ names its page 211 as the source of the line.
1986 — A. C. Weisbecker’s Cosmic Banditos prints the line as an epigraph credited “— Neils Bohr” (Open Library full-text search ↗).
2002 — Edward M. Pavlić’s Crossroads Modernism credits Gribbin and gives the page reference “(211)”, in a passage on what Gribbin calls “The Participatory Universe” (full-text snippet ↗).
2014–2015 — Max Tegmark’s Our Mathematical Universe prints it as “—Niels Bohr” (snippet ↗). Russ Kick’s anthology Flash Wisdom (2015) credits it to “John Gribbin, summarizing Niels Bohr” (snippet ↗).
source.excerptNote: Gribbin’s page could not be read online. The Google Books preview did not show the text, and the Internet Archive scan is lending-only. So only the sentence itself is shown here, not its surrounding paragraph. A 2002 study by Edward M. Pavlić quotes it as Gribbin’s, in a passage on what Gribbin calls “The Participatory Universe,” and gives the page reference “(211).”

author.name: John Gribbin
author.heading: Who John Gribbin is
author.bio: John Gribbin (born 19 March 1946) is a British science writer and astrophysicist and a visiting fellow in astronomy at the University of Sussex. His 1984 book In Search of Schrödinger’s Cat: Quantum Physics and Reality explains quantum theory and its rival interpretations for general readers. Wikiquote identifies it as the real source of this line.

misattribution.heading: Why it gets pinned on Bohr
misattribution.intro: Gribbin wrote the line while explaining Bohr’s quantum ideas, and it reads like a Bohr paradox. Quote collections and books soon dropped Gribbin’s name and kept Bohr’s.

items.scope: Quote sites, social media, many books
items.why: This is the usual credit, but no Bohr paper, lecture, letter or interview with this wording has been identified. Wikiquote’s Bohr page ↗ lists it under “Misattributed” and says it is actually from Gribbin’s book.

items.who: Max Tegmark and Marcus du Sautoy (as Bohr)
items.why: Tegmark’s Our Mathematical Universe prints the line with “—Niels Bohr” (snippet ↗). Wikiquote ↗ also names du Sautoy’s The Great Unknown among the books that credit Bohr.
By 1986 the novel already used the line as an epigraph signed “— Neils Bohr” (Open Library full-text search ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The words are John Gribbin’s, from In Search of Schrödinger’s Cat (1984), p. 211, according to Wikiquote ↗. They describe Bohr’s view, but they are not his words.

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: Gribbin’s In Search of Schrödinger’s Cat was a widely read 1984 introduction to quantum physics and its competing interpretations. Pavlić quotes the line from the book’s discussion of what Gribbin calls “The Participatory Universe”. That is the idea that the quantum world has no definite reality apart from observation.

The sentence sums up that view so neatly that readers took it for a direct quotation from Bohr, the leading voice of the Copenhagen interpretation. Even a 2015 anthology that names Gribbin describes it as Gribbin “summarizing Niels Bohr”.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator has no article on this line. Wikiquote’s sourced finding is the anchor here: it lists the line as misattributed to Bohr and gives Gribbin’s book, p. 211, as the source.

Gribbin’s own page could not be read directly. The Google Books preview showed no text, and the Internet Archive scan is lending-only and not full-text searchable. Two independent books that quote the line support Wikiquote’s citation: Pavlić’s Crossroads Modernism (2002) credits Gribbin with the page reference “(211)”, and Kick’s Flash Wisdom (2015) credits Gribbin.
context.pull: A science writer’s summary of Bohr, later quoted as Bohr himself.
